seasons.name: Cold weather
seasons.intro: The cold weather is the touring season — the district expects to see the sahib on the road, not behind a desk.

seasons.name: Hot weather
seasons.intro: The plains bake. Those who can have fled to the hills; the work shrinks to headquarters and the long, solitary evenings.

seasons.name: The monsoon
seasons.intro: The rains have come. The roads are turning to rivers, the river is rising, and the whole district holds its breath.

tour.label: Go out on tour
tour.note: Among the people — the district steadies; your files and your health do not.

desk.label: Hold the cutcherry
desk.note: Simla’s files clear — but out in the district, unheard, things fester.

kcie.title: The K.C.I.E.
kcie.text: You are gazetted a Knight Commander of the Order of the Indian Empire and become, at thirty-odd, ‘Sir.’ Promoted to Commissioner, mentioned in despatches, permitted to add letters to your name. You have learned nothing, and you will go far. Chhota Nagra is already forgetting you, which is the highest compliment it knows how to pay.

csi.title: The C.S.I.
csi.text: The New Year Honours make you a Companion of the Most Exalted Order of the Star of India — Heaven's Light Our Guide. It is the rarer ribbon, given for a district governed firmly and, against the odds, decently. The Commissioner is faintly puzzled that a man so liked by the governed should be so rewarded. You decide not to explain.

cie.title: The C.I.E.
cie.text: The Gazette records you a Companion of the Order of the Indian Empire — the honest workhorse ribbon of a district man who kept the show on the road. No knighthood, no legend: a competent posting, decently done. In the Service, that is quietly understood to be the whole of the job.

transfer.title: The Quiet Transfer
transfer.text: You are moved to a district even smaller and hotter than this one. No enquiry, no honours, no explanation. This is the Service's way of forgetting a man without the paperwork of dismissing him.

scandal.title: The Scandal
scandal.text: A question is asked in the wrong quarter, a file is opened, and your name travels to London faster than you ever will. You are recalled. At the Club, the subscription list quietly loses your name between one week and the next.

breakdown.title: Invalided Home
breakdown.text: You are put aboard a P&O steamer ‘on grounds of health,’ which is true in the way that all the best official lies are true. The heat, they will say. It is always the heat. You will not come back.

riot.title: A Commission of Enquiry
riot.text: The lathi-charge does not go as the sub-inspector promised. A crowd becomes a headline; a headline becomes a Commission. You spend your last weeks in Chhota Nagra composing a version of events that no one, including you, believes.

bankrupt.title: The Empty Treasury
bankrupt.text: The revenue does not come in, and an Empire runs on revenue coming in. Lala Hukum Chand holds the district's debts and, it emerges, a good deal of yours. You are relieved of a post you could no longer afford to hold.

gonenative.title: Gone Native
gonenative.text: You resign, in terms the Commissioner calls ‘intemperate’ and Pandit Girdhari calls ‘a beginning.’ You are henceforth spoken of as a man who let the side down. It is the only ending this district will remember with anything like affection.

events.title: The Matter of the Sacred Bull
events.body: Sub-Inspector Diwan Chand petitions, with immense dignity, that a Brahminy bull — holy, enormous, and wholly above the law — has for the third time eaten the marigolds he had grown for the flower show. He requests that the bull be, in his words, ‘officially discouraged.’

choices.label: Solemnly issue a written order that the bull be kept off official flowerbeds.
choices.outcome: The order is framed and hung in the police lines. The bull cannot read it. Everyone is nonetheless satisfied that Something Has Been Done.

choices.label: Have the bull quietly relocated to a distant village.
choices.outcome: The village it is relocated to takes the arrival of a holy bull as an omen, and a deputation arrives within the week to ask what they have done to deserve it.

choices.label: Refuse to involve the district administration in bovine theology.
choices.outcome: Correct, dignified, and entirely useless. Diwan Chand's marigolds are eaten a fourth time. He does not forgive you, but he does respect you, which is worse.

events.title: The Billiards Subscription
events.body: An extraordinary meeting of the Chhota Nagra Club is convened over a proposal to raise the billiards subscription by four annas. Mrs. Fortescue-Vane is for. Major Prewitt is violently against. Both look to you, the new Magistrate, to settle a question that has already ended two friendships.

choices.label: Side with Mrs. Fortescue-Vane. One does not cross her.
choices.outcome: You are now, invisibly and permanently, Mrs. Fortescue-Vane's man. This is worth more than a knighthood and costs roughly the same in dignity.

choices.label: Side with Major Prewitt and the principle of the thing.
choices.outcome: The Major shakes your hand as though you have relieved Mafeking. Mrs. Fortescue-Vane says nothing at all, which is how you know.

choices.label: Propose a sub-committee to study the matter.
choices.outcome: You have discovered the single most powerful instrument of British administration: the postponement of a decision until everyone has forgotten why they cared.

events.title: The Revenue Is Short
events.body: A telegram from Commissioner Blyth-Curram, who communicates exclusively in telegrams and disappointment: REVENUE RETURNS CHHOTA NAGRA UNSATISFACTORY STOP EXPECT IMPROVEMENT STOP NO EXCUSES REGARDING RAINFALL WILL BE ENTERTAINED STOP. The rains, it should be said, have failed.

choices.label: Press the collection hard. Simla wants numbers.
choices.outcome: The numbers improve. So does the queue outside Lala Hukum Chand's door, as cultivators borrow at ruinous interest to pay a revenue the fields did not grow.

choices.label: Quietly grant remissions and massage the paperwork.
choices.outcome: You have committed the administrator's original sin: mercy off the books. If it is never discovered you are a good officer. If it is, you are a bad one. The difference is entirely a matter of discovery.

choices.label: Send Simla a magnificent report explaining the rainfall.
choices.outcome: Blyth-Curram replies: RAINFALL NOTED STOP REVENUE STILL SHORT STOP. You have learned that a telegram is not a conversation.

events.title: Pandit Girdhari Holds a Meeting
events.body: Pandit Girdhari Lal, pleader and Congress man, proposes to address a public meeting on the subject of the salt tax, self-rule, and — the intelligence report notes with alarm — ‘the general condition of things.’ It is entirely peaceful. It is also entirely legal. Both facts are considered a nuisance.

choices.label: Ban the meeting under Section 144. Order is order.
choices.outcome: The meeting does not happen. The reason it did not happen is now a far more effective piece of Congress propaganda than the meeting could ever have been. The Pandit sends you a note of thanks. You suspect he is not joking.

choices.label: Permit it, and send a clerk to take dull notes.
choices.outcome: Nothing happens. Speeches are made, the crowd disperses for tea, and the whole apparatus of sedition proves to run, like everything else here, on the assumption that it will be tolerated.

choices.label: Attend personally and sit in the front row.
choices.outcome: Your presence is so unexpected that the Pandit revises his speech on the spot to be scrupulously polite. You understand perhaps one word in five, and both of you leave convinced you have won.

events.title: Lala Hukum Chand Pays a Call
events.body: Lala Hukum Chand — moneylender, landholder, and the man to whom most of the district is quietly mortgaged — calls to pay his respects. He brings a basket of remarkable mangoes and mentions, in passing and with great delicacy, that a certain land dispute might be settled ‘to everyone's satisfaction’ with a word from your court.

choices.label: Accept the mangoes; ignore the hint.
choices.outcome: You have eaten the mangoes and taken none of the meaning, which the Lala finds both admirable and slightly stupid. He will try again, better, later.

choices.label: Decline the mangoes and the man, coldly.
choices.outcome: Incorruptible and lonely. The Lala's money oils every wheel in the district, and you have just introduced a little sand. Things will run slower now, and you will not know why.

choices.label: Have the mangoes; drop a helpful word in court.
choices.outcome: The dispute is settled to the Lala's satisfaction. You are now, in a small and deniable way, his. It is astonishing how light the first thread feels.

events.title: Deputy Collector Mukherjee Is Right Again
events.body: Sub-Deputy Collector Mukherjee — your Indian deputy, Cambridge-educated, visibly cleverer than you, and far too well-mannered to say so — points out, very gently, that the drainage scheme you approved yesterday will flood the very quarter it was meant to protect. He is, of course, correct.

choices.label: Thank him publicly and change the scheme.
choices.outcome: The scheme is fixed. The clerks note that the Magistrate takes correction from an Indian officer, and file the observation somewhere it may one day be useful to somebody.

choices.label: Change the scheme; take the credit yourself.
choices.outcome: The quarter stays dry and your reputation stays high. Mukherjee says nothing, and remembers everything, and remains more competent than you, which is the one thing you cannot fix.

choices.label: Overrule him. A sahib does not reverse himself before the office.
choices.outcome: The quarter floods on schedule. You were right about appearances and wrong about drainage, and the water does not care which.

events.title: The Tiger of Rampur
events.body: Villagers from Rampur report a tiger that has taken two goats and a good deal of sleep. They ask the Magistrate-sahib, as tradition demands, to shoot it. You have fired a rifle four times in your life, twice by accident. The whole district is, however, watching to see whether the new sahib is a shikari or a clerk.

choices.label: Go out and shoot it yourself. It is expected.

ifTrue.outcome: By a miracle compounded of luck and a very close range, the tiger falls. You are, from this fortnight, a pukka sahib in the fullest sense. You are also never going to do that again.

ifFalse.outcome: Your nerves, already frayed, betray you. The tiger escapes; the story does not. A magistrate who cannot shoot straight is a magistrate the district has quietly stopped fearing.

choices.label: Send for a professional shikari from the next district.
choices.outcome: The tiger is dealt with, efficiently and by somebody else. Rampur is grateful and faintly disappointed. A sahib who sends for help is a useful sort of man, but not a legend.

choices.label: Declare it a matter for the Forest Department.
choices.outcome: Correct procedure. The Forest Department will attend to the tiger in the fullness of time, by which the tiger and everyone in Rampur understand: never.

events.title: The Long Evening
events.body: It is nine o'clock, the punkah has stopped because the punkah-wallah has fallen asleep, and you are alone in a bungalow the size of a barn with a bottle of Scotch and eleven hundred miles between you and anyone who knew you before India. The bottle, at least, is company.

choices.label: Pour a large one. And another. It is that or the silence.
choices.outcome: The evening softens. So, over the months, does something else. This is how the district's more famous ruins began — not with a scandal, but with a nightcap that grew steadily larger and started earlier.

choices.label: Pour a small one and write letters home you won't post.
choices.outcome: You describe an India that does not exist to people who would not understand the one that does. It helps. The unsent letters go in the drawer with the others.

choices.label: Go to bed sober and lie awake in the heat.
choices.outcome: Virtue, and the ceiling, keep you company until two. In the morning you are correct, upright, and hollow-eyed, which the office takes for dedication.

events.title: The Rains Have Failed
events.body: There is no rain, and there will be no rain, and the district knows what that word means better than any word in the revenue code. Grain prices climb; the first families sell their cooking pots; a relief works could be opened, but relief works cost money the treasury does not have and Simla did not budget for.

choices.label: Open relief works at once and account for it later.
choices.outcome: Grain-for-labour on the roads and tanks. People do not starve, which no one will thank you for, because averted disasters leave no monument. The treasury, however, remembers.

choices.label: Wait for sanction from Simla before spending a rupee.
choices.outcome: You follow procedure exactly. Sanction arrives in six weeks, which is four weeks after it would have mattered. The files are impeccable. The district is not.

choices.label: Lean on Lala Hukum Chand to release grain on credit.
choices.outcome: The grain flows, at the Lala's interest and on the Lala's terms, and the district's debt to him deepens by a generation. You have solved this famine with a promise the next one will have to keep.

events.title: The Commissioner Inspects
events.body: Commissioner Blyth-Curram descends upon Chhota Nagra in person, walrus-moustached and radiating grievance, to inspect the district, the treasury, the lock-up, and you. He will form an opinion in the first ten minutes and spend the visit confirming it. The whole station has been whitewashed, including, it is rumoured, several things that were not walls.

choices.label: Show him a flawless, rehearsed district.
choices.outcome: Every ledger balances, every prisoner is suspiciously cheerful, every road has been mended along precisely the stretch he will drive. He leaves satisfied. The performance has cost you a fortnight and a small piece of your soul, both of which the Service considers a fair price.

choices.label: Show him the real district, warts and all.
choices.outcome: You show him the flooded quarter, the short revenue, the honest mess of the thing. He is appalled by your candour and, in a corner of his walrus heart he will never admit to, faintly impressed. It will not help your career. It may help you sleep.

choices.label: Ply him with the Club's best brandy and change the subject.
choices.outcome: By the second brandy he is telling you about his own first district; by the third, the inspection is effectively over. You have learned that the Empire, at its highest levels, runs substantially on the avoidance of awkwardness.

events.title: Fever in the Bazaar
events.body: A fever — the Civil Surgeon says cholera, the bazaar says worse — appears in the crowded lanes behind the grain market. The Surgeon wants the quarter cordoned and the wells closed. The traders want the market open. The pilgrims want to keep moving. Everyone wants you to choose, so that there will be someone to blame.

choices.label: Cordon the quarter and close the wells. Public health first.
choices.outcome: The fever is contained; the trade is throttled; the traders write to Simla about the high-handed young Magistrate. You saved lives and made enemies, and only one of those two things generates correspondence.

choices.label: Keep the market open and hope the Surgeon is exaggerating.
choices.outcome: The market thrives for eleven days. On the twelfth, the Surgeon is proved right in the way that surgeons are proved right, and the cordon you refused to order becomes a cordon you cannot make wide enough.

choices.label: Split the difference: cordon quietly, keep up appearances.
choices.outcome: You do half of what the Surgeon asked and claim to have done all of it and none of it, depending on the audience. The fever, indifferent to your positioning, does slightly less than its worst.

events.title: A Question of Precedence
events.body: At the Club's cold-weather ball, a furious dispute erupts over the order of precedence at dinner — specifically, whether the Executive Engineer's wife outranks the Forest Officer's wife. It is, everyone agrees, a trivial matter. It is also, everyone understands, a matter that could poison the entire station for a season.

choices.label: Rule strictly by the Warrant of Precedence.
choices.outcome: You produce the actual Warrant of Precedence, an object roughly as sacred here as scripture, and settle the matter by the book. Both wives are furious, but at the book, which cannot be invited to dinner or snubbed at it.

choices.label: Seat them apart and pretend it was always so.
choices.outcome: A little diplomatic fiction, gracefully deployed. The ball proceeds. You have discovered that the skills of a District Magistrate and the skills of a nervous head waiter are, at the Club, precisely identical.

choices.label: Declare you will not adjudicate the seating of a dinner.
choices.outcome: Principled, and a grave misreading of the room. At a frontier station the seating of a dinner is the government. By declining to rule, you have not risen above the station's politics; you have merely lost them.

events.title: The Case of the Stolen Buffalo
events.body: A cultivator stands accused of stealing his neighbour's buffalo. The evidence is a tangle of perjury on both sides, the village is split, and the truth — that the buffalo wandered and both men are lying about the rest — is not available in any form the law can use. Both families are watching your face for the verdict.

choices.label: Convict on the letter of the evidence.
choices.outcome: You convict the man the paperwork points to, who is probably guilty of something, if not this. The law is served. Justice files no return and is not consulted.

choices.label: Acquit for reasonable doubt and return the buffalo.
choices.outcome: You cut the knot: doubt to the accused, buffalo to its likely owner, a small homily to both families. Nobody is fully satisfied, which in a village dispute is the surest sign of a fair result.

choices.label: Bind both parties over and make them share the beast.
choices.outcome: Solomon in a solar topi. The two families are bound to joint custody of one bad-tempered buffalo, an arrangement so mutually inconvenient that they are reconciled by the shared grievance within the year.

events.title: A New Form Is Required
events.body: Simla, in its wisdom, introduces Form XIV-B, to be completed in quintuplicate, recording the caste, occupation, and ‘general disposition’ of every petitioner appearing before the court. Ram Autar, your head clerk, lays it before you with the particular stillness he reserves for orders that are both compulsory and insane.

choices.label: Implement it fully. An order is an order.
choices.outcome: The office vanishes beneath quintuplicate. Justice slows to the speed of carbon paper. Simla, receiving its forms on time, concludes that Chhota Nagra is a model of efficiency, which is the exact opposite of the truth and precisely what the forms were designed to produce.

choices.label: Have Ram Autar fill them in plausibly and file the rest.
choices.outcome: Ram Autar's face does not move, but something in the office relaxes. A quiet compact is formed: he will manufacture the paperwork the Empire requires, and you will not ask how. It is the most useful alliance you will make in India.

choices.label: Write to Simla objecting to Form XIV-B on principle.
choices.outcome: You receive Form XIV-B-1, a supplementary form on which to record objections to Form XIV-B. The machine has met your resistance and grown a new part to digest it.

events.title: Ram Autar Has a Nephew
events.body: Ram Autar, your invaluable head clerk, mentions with exquisite indirection that his sister's son is a promising young man in want of a clerkship, and that a vacancy happens to exist in the tahsil office. Everything Ram Autar does for you depends on a web of exactly such small arrangements. So, you are beginning to realise, does everything.

choices.label: Appoint the nephew. Ram Autar has earned it.
choices.outcome: The nephew is appointed and turns out to be perfectly competent, which is not the point. The point is that you now understand how the district is actually staffed, and that the answer has nothing to do with the rules and everything to do with Ram Autar.

choices.label: Insist on open competition for the post.
choices.outcome: You hold a fair examination, which the nephew wins anyway, having been the only serious candidate Ram Autar permitted to apply. You have upheld a principle and changed nothing, at some cost to a friendship you could not afford to spend.

events.title: The Camp at Rampur
events.body: Your tents are pitched under a mango tope outside Rampur; the patwari’s land-records are spread on the camp table, the headman is anxious, and a queue of cultivators has formed to lay grievances before the sahib in person. This is the district as it actually is, not as the files describe it.

choices.label: Go through the land records line by line with the patwari.
choices.outcome: You find three fields recorded to men who died in the last famine and one to a man who never existed. The patwari is either a rogue or an artist; either way the records are truer tonight than they were this morning.

choices.label: Hear the cultivators’ grievances under the mango tree.
choices.outcome: You sit until dark hearing of a bad well, a hard landlord, a boundary that has walked in the night. You can mend perhaps one grievance in five, but being heard by the sahib is itself a kind of remedy, and the village knows it.

choices.label: Keep it brief — show the flag and move on.
choices.outcome: You are seen, saluted, and gone by noon. The tour register records a village inspected. What the village records is that the sahib did not stay to listen.

events.title: A Letter from the Hills
events.body: The hot weather is on, the plains are an oven, and a letter comes down from the hill station where your wife has taken the children for the season. She asks, not for the first time, when you will come up for your local leave — and whether it is not time the boy was sent Home to school in England, as everyone’s children are.

choices.label: Take your local leave and go up to the hills.
choices.outcome: A fortnight of cool air and your own family, and of pretending you are not thinking about the district. You come down restored and faintly guilty. The work waited; it always waits; that is the one dependable thing about it.

choices.label: Stay at your post; agree the boy goes Home.
choices.outcome: You sign the letter that sends your son across an ocean to be raised by a school and an aunt, for his health and his accent and his prospects. It is what the Service does to its families. You tell yourself it is for the best, and go back to the files.

choices.label: Stay, and put the decision off another year.
choices.outcome: You write a warm, evasive letter and post it up the hill. Nothing is decided, which is its own kind of decision. The heat presses on the bungalow like a hand.

events.title: The Hot Weather
events.body: By May the thermometer stands at a hundred and ten in the shade, the station has half-emptied for the hills, the punkahs never stop, and the nights are worse than the days. This is the season that breaks men quietly — the loo wind, the glare, and the long solitary evenings with nothing between you and the silence but a bottle and the ceiling.

choices.label: Keep to a rigid routine — dawn rides, cold baths, work.
choices.outcome: Discipline is the sahib’s armour against the heat. You ride at dawn, work through the shuttered day, and hold yourself together by the timetable. It is joyless, and it works.

choices.label: Let the Club and the bottle carry you through.
choices.outcome: The little society of the half-empty station closes ranks around its bar. The evenings pass more easily; the mornings less so. It is the well-worn road, and you can see from here where it leads.

choices.label: Drive yourself at the work to fill the emptiness.
choices.outcome: You bury the silence under files and clear a backlog two years deep. Simla is pleased. Something in you is being spent that no honours list will ever repay.

events.title: The River Comes Up
events.body: Three days of rain and the river is over its banks; the low villages are islands, the rail embankment is the only high ground for miles, and a crowd of the flooded-out is gathering on it with their cattle and their cooking pots. Boats are few, the night is coming on, and the water is still rising.

choices.label: Take personal charge of the rescue from a boat.
choices.outcome: You spend two nights on the water pulling families off rooftops, soaked and sleepless and more use than you have felt in months. The district will long remember that the sahib came himself. So, unfortunately, will your constitution.

choices.label: Organise from the embankment — relief camp, grain, order.
choices.outcome: You set up the relief camp, commandeer the grain, and keep a frightened crowd from becoming a mob. Unglamorous, competent, and precisely the job. Nobody drowns who can be reached; some cannot be reached.

choices.label: Wire for military help and hold the line till it comes.
choices.outcome: The sappers arrive with boats on the second day and do the work you could not. It is the sensible call, and the district notes that in its worst hour the sahib sent a telegram and waited. Sense is rarely forgiven.

events.title: The Procession and the Mosque
events.body: The great autumn procession of one community is due to pass, as it has for a century, down the lane that runs past the other community's chief mosque at the hour of prayer. Both parties have come to your cutcherry — one citing custom, one citing insult — and both have brought enough young men to make plain that this is no longer only a question of a route.

choices.label: Order the procession to keep its ancient route.
choices.outcome: You uphold custom and brace for it. The procession passes; there is shoving, a thrown brick, a lathi-charge that stops just short of a headline. Custom is preserved, and everyone is now quite certain that next year will be worse.

choices.label: Divert the procession by a longer, quieter road.
choices.outcome: You reroute it in the name of peace. One community mutters that the sahib has broken a hundred years of right; the other says nothing, and remembers that the sahib can be moved. You have bought the peace of this year with the authority of the next.

choices.label: Summon both sides and broker a compromise yourself.
choices.outcome: You spend three exhausting days hammering out a route, a timing, and a face-saving fiction for each side. It holds. It is the hardest and least visible work there is, and the only kind that leaves a district quieter than you found it.

events.title: The Dacoits of the Ravines
events.body: A gang has come up out of the ravine country — three villages robbed, a moneylender's house burned, and a growing suspicion among the cultivators that the sahib's writ stops where the good roads do. The Superintendent wants a sweep; the villages want protection; the dacoits, by all accounts, want to become a legend.

choices.label: Lead an armed sweep of the ravines in person.
choices.outcome: You spend a fortnight in the saddle in bad country and the gang scatters — two taken, one shot, the rest gone across the border. The ravines are quiet, your constitution less so, and the legend, annoyingly, only grows.

choices.label: Work quietly through informers and moneylenders.
choices.outcome: Money changes hands in the dark and, in time, so does information. The gang is broken from within — cheaper and cleverer than a sweep, and winning no one any medals, least of all you.

choices.label: Post a reward and leave it to the police.
choices.outcome: You do the correct, distant thing. The poster is much admired; the dacoits are not caught; the ravine villages draw the obvious conclusion about how far the sahib will actually ride for them.

events.title: The District Budget
events.body: The annual estimates are due at the Secretariat, and the district's slender purse must be divided between the things that keep people alive, the things that keep people quiet, and the things that keep Simla content. Ram Autar lays three drafts before you, each balanced, each a small betrayal of the other two.

choices.label: Fund public works — wells, roads, a dispensary.
choices.outcome: You spend on the unglamorous things a district actually needs. The wells get dug, the people are quietly better off, and the Secretariat notes that your establishment charges creep above the provincial average. One of these facts will follow you; guess which.

choices.label: Economise and return a surplus to the province.
choices.outcome: You hand Simla a tidy surplus and your district a leaking tank and a shut dispensary. The Financial Secretary is delighted. Delight, in the Finance Department, is the highest form of life.

choices.label: Quietly strengthen the police lines.
choices.outcome: You put the money where it buys quiet rather than gratitude. The lock-up is mended, the constables paid on time, and the district grows a little safer and a little more watched. You tell yourself these are the same thing.

events.title: The Zamindar and the Tenants
events.body: The zamindar of Pipariya has enhanced his tenants' rents to a figure the land cannot bear, and the tenants — forty families, and the record on their side for once — have brought it to your court. The zamindar has brought his pleader, his account books, and a pointed reminder that men of property are the natural friends of Government.

choices.label: Rule for the tenants and roll back the rents.
choices.outcome: You cut the rents to what the fields will yield. Forty families bless the sahib; the zamindar writes to the Commissioner about the dangerous radicalism of the young magistrate, and encloses, he regrets, a list of his loyal services to the Crown.

choices.label: Rule for the zamindar — a contract is a contract.
choices.outcome: You uphold the letter of the lease. The revenue is secured, the men of property reassured, and forty families learn exactly where they stand in the order of the sahib's concerns. Some will remember it at the next Congress meeting.

choices.label: Send it to arbitration and split the difference.
choices.outcome: You appoint arbitrators and land on a rent that pinches everyone equally. Neither side is happy, the record is muddied past appeal, and the essential business of the Raj — the postponement of a reckoning — is once more served.

events.title: A School for Sonpur
events.body: On tour you are met at Sonpur by villagers who have, astonishingly, built a schoolhouse with their own hands and their own rupees, and now ask only that Government supply a master and his salary. It is precisely the self-help the annual report always praises, and precisely the recurring charge the Finance Department exists to prevent.

choices.label: Sanction the master and the salary at once.
choices.outcome: You sign the sanction on the spot, to the frank astonishment of the deputation, who had budgeted a year of petitions for it. Sonpur gets its school. It is the rarest official pleasure: a small good done quickly, before anyone can explain why it can't be.

choices.label: Forward it through channels with a warm note.
choices.outcome: You do it properly, which is to say slowly. The file begins its long pilgrimage through the Education Department. The schoolhouse waits, empty and swept, a small monument to the distance between a village and the Secretariat.

choices.label: Praise their spirit and make no promises.
choices.outcome: You give them a handsome speech about self-reliance and no master. They built a school on the strength of the sahib's justice; they will draw their own conclusions about the strength of the sahib's word.

events.title: The Boycott of Foreign Cloth
events.body: Bonfires of Manchester cloth are being lit in the bazaar, and the mill-agents and box-wallahs — loyal men, taxpayers, the backbone of the revenue — demand that you stop this seditious burning of perfectly good imported goods. The cloth is, inconveniently, the burners' own property.

choices.label: Ban the bonfires as a breach of the peace.
choices.outcome: You forbid the burnings and thereby confirm, for anyone who doubted it, that the Government of India regards the burning of a man's own shirt as a threat to the Empire. The box-wallahs are grateful. The nationalist press could not have scripted you better.

choices.label: Permit it — a man may burn his own cloth.
choices.outcome: You decline to defend Manchester from the citizens of Chhota Nagra. The bonfires burn out on their own, as bonfires do, and the mill-agents write to the Chamber of Commerce about the alarming sympathies of the local magistrate.

choices.label: Look the other way and buy some khadi yourself.
choices.outcome: You have a homespun coat quietly made and wear it on tour. It is comfortable, it is a small treason, and Ram Autar's face when he sees it is the nearest thing to open emotion he has shown all year.

events.title: A Scandal at the Club
events.body: In the dead of the hot weather, with tempers and thermometers both past bearing, young Pemberton of the Police has been discovered in a compromising arrangement involving another man's wife, a great deal of the Club's whisky, and a challenge shouted across the billiard room. As the senior civil officer present, the mess of it lands, inevitably, on you.

choices.label: Hush it up and send Pemberton on sudden leave.
choices.outcome: You engineer a discreet transfer and a story about his health, and the station agrees, as stations do, to have seen nothing. The appearances are saved. Somewhere under them, everyone knows exactly what happened, which is the ordinary condition of station life.

choices.label: Report it properly up the chain.
choices.outcome: You do the honest thing and put it on paper. Pemberton's career ends; the wronged husband is not mollified; and the station marks you down as a man who cannot be trusted to keep a thing quiet — the one unforgivable sin at a small mess.

choices.label: Bang heads together and settle it over brandy.
choices.outcome: You lock the three of them in the card-room and do not let them out until there is an apology, a handshake, and a shared understanding that the alternative is you. It works, at some cost to your evening and to your faith in the ruling race.

events.title: Lala Hukum Chand Calls It In
events.body: The mangoes are long eaten, and the Lala has come to collect on the goodwill he so carefully planted. Nothing so crude as the money, he assures you — merely a small matter: a rival trader whose licence might be found irregular, a word in the right ledger. He smiles. Outside, the district you both govern goes about its business, not knowing which of you it belongs to.

choices.label: Do the small thing he asks. It is small.
choices.outcome: The rival's licence is found wanting; the Lala's ledger is squared; a little of your debt is quietly forgiven. It was small, exactly as he said, and that is how it is done — never one large sin, always a series of small ones, each easier than the last.

choices.label: Refuse him, and let the debt stand.
choices.outcome: You decline, politely, and watch the warmth leave the room. The debt is called to its full figure, and his money leaves the wheels of your district un-oiled overnight. You have kept your honour. It will prove a more expensive possession than you imagined.

choices.label: Repay him in full from the chest and be free.
choices.outcome: You empty a dangerous share of the treasury to buy back your own hands. The Lala takes his money with a bow that conveys precisely how much more useful the debt would have been to him than the cash. You are poorer, and free, and those turn out to be connected.

events.title: The District Stops Work
events.body: What began with Pandit Girdhari's banned meeting has become a hartal — the shops shuttered, the courts empty, the very peons of your own cutcherry finding urgent reasons to be elsewhere. It is disciplined, it is peaceful, and it frightens the Secretariat far more than a riot would, because a riot can at least be charged.

choices.label: Break the strike under the emergency powers.
choices.outcome: You invoke the ordinances, arrest the organisers, and reopen the shops at the point of persuasion. Order returns to the surface of things. Underneath, something has changed no ordinance addresses: the district has learned it can stop, all together, whenever it chooses.

choices.label: Wait it out and let the hartal exhaust itself.
choices.outcome: You do nothing, magnificently, for eleven days, while Simla's telegrams grow shriller. The strike ends of its own weight, having proved its point precisely by your inability to prevent it. Blyth-Curram will remember that you sat on your hands. So will the Pandit.

choices.label: Meet the Pandit and offer a real concession.
choices.outcome: You do the thing no one in Simla forgives: you treat with him as a man with a case. You give a little — a committee, a hearing, a grievance actually addressed — and the shutters go up. You have kept your district and quite possibly ended your career, and you are no longer sure those are different things.

events.title: What Ram Autar Knew
events.body: An anonymous petition, in a clerk's careful hand, lays out how the head clerk's small arrangements have grown over the years into something the audit would call embezzlement and the district calls simply how things are done. Ram Autar has run your office, saved your reputation a dozen times, and, it seems, taken his tithe of all that passed through it. He awaits your decision with the stillness he shows a compulsory order.

choices.label: Bury the petition. He has earned that much.
choices.outcome: You feed the petition to the brazier and say nothing. The office runs on as before, and you understand at last that you did not buy Ram Autar's loyalty — you rented it, and this is the rent. He pours your tea next morning exactly as always. You cannot meet his eye; he does not require you to.

choices.label: Confront him privately and demand it stop.
choices.outcome: You put it to him quietly and he neither denies nor apologises; he simply, gravely, agrees. The skimming stops. So does a great deal of the frictionless magic by which your office used to work, for it turns out the two ran through the same quiet pipes.

choices.label: Report him. The law is the law.
choices.outcome: You do the clean, correct, ruinous thing. Ram Autar is suspended pending enquiry, and within a fortnight you discover how much of the district lived in his head and nowhere else. You have upheld the law and lost the man who made your rule possible. The files are honest now. They are also three weeks behind.

events.title: A Letter from the School
events.body: A letter comes, months old, in a round schoolboy hand already becoming a stranger's. Your son is well, is learning Latin, has been caned once (unjustly), and asks — without quite asking — when you are coming Home. Between the lines a housemaster has added that the boy is settling, which is the word the English use for a wound that has stopped bleeding.

choices.label: Write back at once, warmly, and promise a visit.
choices.outcome: You fill a page with a leave you cannot yet take and a green English field he half-remembers. It costs nothing to promise and steadies you to imagine it. Whether the promise survives contact with the Secretariat's leave-sanction is another year's grief.

choices.label: Send money and a stiff word of encouragement.
choices.outcome: You do what your own father did, in the same climate, for the same reasons, and tell yourself it made a man of you. The letter is correct and cold, and you know it even as you seal it, and you seal it anyway. The heat presses on the bungalow like a hand.

choices.label: Pour a drink and leave it unanswered.
choices.outcome: You mean to answer it tomorrow. Tomorrow the district has a fresh demand, and the letter migrates to the drawer with the others you mean to answer, and something between you and the boy lengthens by another silence. This, too, is how it is done.

events.title: The Commissioner's Durbar
events.body: A grand durbar is to be held — the Commissioner presiding, the district's notables assembled by rank, robes of honour distributed, loyalty affirmed, and the whole elaborate theatre of the Raj staged for an afternoon in the maidan. Your task is the seating: a chair too high or too low, a name called out of order, and a feud is born that will outlive you.

choices.label: Stage it flawlessly by the Warrant and the old lists.
choices.outcome: Every notable is seated to the inch of his dignity, every robe bestowed on cue, and the durbar unfolds like clockwork wound by a nervous man. The Commissioner is pleased; the notables placated; you have spent a week of your life on a seating plan and would, appallingly, do it again.

choices.label: Use the seating to reward the loyal, cool the awkward.
choices.outcome: You quietly promote the friends of Government up the rows and let the difficult men feel the draught from the back. It is deftly done and widely understood, and you have turned an afternoon of pageantry into a small, sharp instrument of rule. The Pandit, uninvited, is said to have laughed.

choices.label: Keep it plain and spend the saving on the district.
choices.outcome: You stage a modest durbar and divert the saved expense to a relief fund. The notables are faintly insulted to be honoured on a budget; the district notices that the sahib would rather feed it than flatter it. Only one of those constituencies writes the confidential reports.
